Xen should sit above every individual Claude account and every individual Claude session. Xen is the persistent system. Claude accounts are just replaceable workers underneath it. It should not create a new Xen identity, restart discovery, or rebuild context from scratch. It should continue from the same persistent Xen goal and the same evidence. The second major component is the durable goal store. Every real objective you give Xen should live outside the Claude session. If one Claude worker disappears, the goal still exists. Another worker resumes it from that store. The third major component is the canonical desired-state manifest. This is a machine-readable representation of what Xen is allowed to be. It should include rules such as God Mode is the canonical tool plane, Session O is deprecated, Xen Context routing is deprecated, voice must not be blocked beyond five seconds, one Xen voice is allowed, Bee/Omi input must not be naïvely deduplicated by common words, raw Akashic evidence must remain available, Lifenote is a projection rather than the source of truth, and no new code may silently replace a proven working path without passing its regression tests. Claude should not be able to edit the desired-state rules and immediately declare itself compliant. Those rules should be owned by a separate control mechanism. The fourth major component is the runtime reconciler. This is a continuously running process that compares what the machine is actually doing against the desired-state manifest. It inspects live processes, launchd jobs, active routes, the current God Mode tool surface, ingress behavior, voice behavior, active Claude workers, and other load-bearing state. If the runtime drifts from the canonical state, the reconciler repairs it or restores the last proven state. Claude can propose a change, but the reconciler decides whether that change is allowed to remain active. The fifth major component is the claim broker. Claude should no longer be able to freely say things like working, fixed, live, delivered, deployed, healthy, or verified based only on its own interpretation. If Claude wants to claim that a browser surface is working, the verifier should inspect the actual rendered browser state. If Claude wants to claim that voice is working, the verifier should confirm the actual audio path. If Claude wants to claim that the five-second governor successfully interrupted a blocker, the verifier should confirm that the exact blocking process released foreground ownership. The verifier then produces a fresh evidence receipt. That receipt should name the exact thing tested, the exact target, the time it was tested, what was expected, what was observed, and how long that proof remains fresh. Only then should Xen be allowed to present the claim as verified. The sixth component is the five-second voice governor. This process must live outside Claude’s normal conversational turn. It should be silent. It should not generate answers. It should not use another model. It should not depend on UserPromptSubmit. It should not rely on Claude cooperating. The governor watches three things continuously: when a real live utterance arrives, whether Xen has serviced it, and which process currently owns the foreground. The moment a live utterance arrives, the governor starts an independent monotonic five-second timer. During those five seconds it continuously identifies the exact process that would have to be interrupted if the utterance remains unserviced. At five seconds exactly, if the utterance is still waiting and an interruptible process is genuinely blocking Xen, the governor directly interrupts that exact process or process group. All external inputs must enter Xen as structured data rather than raw text injected blindly into an executable terminal. Here is the same architecture I was describing, but translated into natural language instead of diagrams/code so playback will read it clearly. Xen should sit above every individual Claude account and every individual Claude session. Xen is the persistent system. Claude accounts are just replaceable workers underneath it. The first major component is the capacity router. Its job is to watch every Claude seat you have and know which one is available, which one is rate-limited, which one has exhausted its current session, which one has weekly capacity left, and which one is currently running work. When one Claude seat becomes unavailable, the router should automatically assign unfinished work to another eligible seat. It should not create a new Xen identity, restart discovery, or rebuild context from scratch. It should continue from the same persistent Xen goal and the same evidence. The second major component is the durable goal store. Every real objective you give Xen should live outside the Claude session. The goal store keeps the goal ID, what the objective is, what has already been completed, what remains open, which worker is currently assigned, what evidence has been produced, and what acceptance criteria are still unmet. If one Claude worker disappears, the goal still exists. Another worker resumes it from that store. The third major component is the canonical desired-state manifest. This is a machine-readable representation of what Xen is allowed to be. It should include rules such as God Mode is the canonical tool plane, Session O is deprecated, Xen Context routing is deprecated, voice must not be blocked beyond five seconds, one Xen voice is allowed, Bee/Omi input must not be naïvely deduplicated by common words, raw Akashic evidence must remain available, Lifenote is a projection rather than the source of truth, and no new code may silently replace a proven working path without passing its regression tests. Claude should not be able to edit the desired-state rules and immediately declare itself compliant. Those rules should be owned by a separate control mechanism. The fourth major component is the runtime reconciler. This is a continuously running process that compares what the machine is actually doing against the desired-state manifest. It inspects live processes, launchd jobs, active routes, the current God Mode tool surface, ingress behavior, voice behavior, active Claude workers, and other load-bearing state. If the runtime drifts from the canonical state, the reconciler repairs it or restores the last proven state. Claude can propose a change, but the reconciler decides whether that change is allowed to remain active. The fifth major component is the claim broker. Claude should no longer be able to freely say things like working, fixed, live, delivered, deployed, healthy, or verified based only on its own interpretation. When Claude wants to make one of those claims, the claim broker requires evidence from an independent verifier. For example, if Claude wants to claim that the MCP endpoint is working, the verifier should make a real tool call against the actual endpoint and inspect the returned body. If Claude wants to claim that a browser surface is working, the verifier should inspect the actual rendered browser state. If Claude wants to claim that voice is working, the verifier should confirm the actual audio path. If Claude wants to claim that the five-second governor successfully interrupted a blocker, the verifier should confirm that the exact blocking process released foreground ownership. The verifier then produces a fresh evidence receipt. That receipt should name the exact thing tested, the exact target, the time it was tested, what was expected, what was observed, and how long that proof remains fresh. Only then should Xen be allowed to present the claim as verified. The sixth component is the five-second voice governor. This process must live outside Claude’s normal conversational turn. It should be silent. It should not generate answers. It should not use another model. It should not depend on UserPromptSubmit. It should not rely on Claude cooperating. The governor watches three things continuously: when a real live utterance arrives, whether Xen has serviced it, and which process currently owns the foreground. The moment a live utterance arrives, the governor starts an independent monotonic five-second timer. During those five seconds it continuously identifies the exact process that would have to be interrupted if the utterance remains unserviced. At five seconds exactly, if the utterance is still waiting and an interruptible process is genuinely blocking Xen, the governor directly interrupts that exact process or process group. It does not send a generic Escape key and assume success. It verifies that the process actually stopped owning the foreground. If it did not, the governor escalates only against that same blocker. Background agents, Comet, compaction, memory indexing, and unrelated shells continue running. The seventh component is the canonical ingress layer. All external inputs must enter Xen as structured data rather than raw text injected blindly into an executable terminal. A Bee message, Omi transcript, notification, SMS, email, browser event, or agent message should arrive with a source, event ID, timestamp, type, payload, and provenance. The system decides whether it is data, user speech, a replay, machine output, or executable control. Arbitrary external prose should never become Bash commands simply because it was routed through tmux. The eighth component is the canonical utterance resolver. Omi, Bee, VEI, and other rails can carry multiple copies of the same spoken utterance. The resolver should decide whether an incoming event is genuinely new speech, a delayed second delivery, a historical replay, summary content, or machine-generated content. It should use message IDs, timestamps, source identity, fingerprints, and provenance. It should not decide that two messages are duplicates just because they share an ordinary word such as okay or no. The ninth component is God Mode, which is the same thing you refer to as underscore god mode, SELMCP, and the endpoint mcp dot xlrd dot org slash mcp. This should be treated as one canonical tool plane, not three separate systems. Before Xen creates a new daemon or service, it should inspect God Mode and determine whether the required capability already exists there. If it exists and works, use it. If it exists and is broken, repair it. If it exists but is incomplete, extend it. Only build something new when the capability is genuinely absent. The tenth component is the deprecated-route eliminator. Xen Context and Session O routing should be treated as deprecated. The system should search for every current dependency on them. Historical references remain in Akashic, but active production code should be migrated away from those routes. There should be no silent fallback from God Mode into Session O or Xen Context. The eleventh component is the Comet semantic adapter. Comet remains Xen’s browser body. Claude owns persistent intent and reasoning. Comet owns current browser state, logged-in applications, navigation, research, and interactive web actions. The adapter should translate between Xen’s durable goals and Comet’s live browser work. If God Mode already exposes browser control primitives, the Comet sidecar should adapt those primitives instead of creating another independent browser automation stack. It should emit events such as connected, disconnected, assistant started, progress, completed, blocked, action started, action completed, refusal, and error. If Comet gets blocked, Claude takes over through God Mode, PTY, MCP, or another agent, solves the blocker, and resumes the same Comet task under the same goal ID. The twelfth component is Akashic. Akashic is the permanent record of what actually happened. It keeps exact PTY and tmux activity, Claude events, Comet actions, browser events, MCP calls, A2A messages, voice transcripts, files, artifacts, failures, recoveries, and derived-memory references. Summaries never replace raw evidence. The thirteenth component is NATS. NATS is only the live event transport. It moves structured events between systems. It does not become the source of truth and it does not become a serial work queue. Akashic remains the authoritative record. The fourteenth component is Lifenote. Lifenote is the human-readable live projection of Akashic. When you look at Lifenote, you should be able to see the exact user speech, what Claude interpreted, which worker acted, which Comet action ran, which shell command executed, what files changed, what evidence was produced, what failed, what recovered, and what the current goal state is. Every summarized item should be expandable back to raw evidence. The fifteenth component is the memory layer. Claude Mem, Bastra Recall, Graphiti, Qdrant, Supabase, or other memory stores should all be treated as projections or retrieval systems underneath Akashic. They should retain source provenance. If one memory system is slow or broken, Xen should fail soft and continue. Memory retrieval must not own the live voice path. The sixteenth component is VVS output ownership. Xen should have one canonical outward response path that controls voice, SMS, and vision. Long responses should be segmented correctly, but every segment of one utterance must belong to the same output ownership tree. Newer user speech should be able to barge in and terminate the entire old utterance tree. Detached voice children should not continue speaking after the conversation has moved on. The seventeenth component is the RVC voice path. The system should independently track whether the RVC process is running, whether the model is loaded, whether the WebSocket is connected, whether PCM audio is entering, whether conversion is happening, whether real-time factor is below one, whether PCM is leaving, whether playback is active, and whether audio was actually heard. A green health endpoint alone should not be allowed to prove voice success. The eighteenth component is the regression gate. Every proposed production change should be treated as a candidate, not immediately as live truth. Before activation, the system should compare the candidate against the last proven runtime and make sure known functionality has not disappeared. It should run the relevant acceptance tests. Only a passing candidate becomes active. If runtime behavior later drifts, the reconciler restores the proven state. The nineteenth component is the evidence ledger. Every meaningful change should record what defect was observed, what source file or process caused it, what patch was made, what test was run, what exact evidence came back, and what the status is. Valid statuses should be verified end to end, code shipped but unverified, externally blocked, or failed. The final structure is this in natural language. Xen is the persistent authority. The Claude accounts are replaceable workers. God Mode is the canonical tool plane. The capacity router chooses available Claude workers. The durable goal store preserves unfinished work independently of those workers. The desired-state manifest says what Xen is allowed to become. The runtime reconciler keeps the real system aligned with that manifest. The five-second governor protects live voice without relying on Claude cooperation. The claim broker prevents Claude from declaring its own success. Independent attestors produce fresh evidence receipts. Canonical ingress prevents external data from becoming executable shell input. The utterance resolver prevents Bee, Omi, and VEI copies from becoming duplicate conversations. Comet remains Xen’s web body. Akashic preserves what actually happened. NATS distributes live events. Lifenote shows you the entire organism in human-readable form. Memory systems derive context from Akashic but never replace it. VVS owns outward communication. RVC owns trained voice transformation. Regression gates prevent a later patch from deleting something that already worked. And the governing idea is this: Claude is allowed to work on Xen. Claude is no longer allowed to be the sole authority that decides whether Xen is correct.

This is the same path we walked start to finish. A developer named Jamie Pine built Voicebox, a free app that clones a voice from one short recording, speaks it back in 23 languages, and plugs into Claude so your AI can answer out loud in your own voice. Everything runs locally on your machine. Here is every step, plus the two things that tripped us up so they do not trip you up. 01 INSTALL VOICEBOX Download Voicebox from voicebox.sh and drag it into Applications. It is a small independent app, so it is not signed by Apple yet. The first time you open it, macOS will block it. Do not fight the popup. Go to System Settings, then Privacy and Security, scroll to the bottom, and click Open Anyway. That is it, it opens every time after that. If you would rather do it in one line, run this in Terminal first: sudo xattr -rd com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Voicebox.app 02 DOWNLOAD THE RIGHT ENGINE Voicebox ships seven voice engines and this is the one place people pick wrong. Only one engine both clones a voice from a sample and covers all 23 languages: Chatterbox Multilingual. Ai Actionable AI T H E A C T I O N A B L E A I. C O M A C T I O N A B L E A I · T H E A C T I O N A B L E A I. C O M Clone Your Voice And Give It To Your AI, Free And Local The exact setup we used to clone a voice in one recording, speak it in 23 languages, and wire it into Claude so your AI talks back to you in your own voice. All of it runs on your own Mac, nothing in the cloud. → The one engine inside Voicebox that actually clones a voice and does all 23 languages → The recording trick that decides whether your clone sounds alive or dead flat → The single command that lets Claude speak its answers back to you in your voice Open the Models tab and download Chatterbox Multilingual. Wait for it to finish before you generate anything. If you use the default engine instead, cloning either falls back to a generic voice or fails outright. Chatterbox Multilingual is the one that does the magic. 03 CLONE YOUR VOICE Go to Profiles, click New Profile, name it, and set the engine to Chatterbox Multilingual. Then record or upload one clean sample of your voice, 15 to 30 seconds is plenty. Save it and the clone is ready in seconds. The part nobody tells you The clone copies HOW you talk, not just how you sound. If you record your sample reading flat and careful, every single output comes out flat and lifeless. We learned this the hard way. Record your sample with real energy, like you are telling a friend something exciting. Smile while you do it, let your pitch move around. Whatever emotion you put into the sample is the emotion you get back. 04 SPEAK IN ANY LANGUAGE Type any text, pick your profile, and generate. Here is the one thing to understand: the language selector does not translate your words, it only sets the accent and pronunciation. So to speak real Spanish in your voice, you first put Spanish text in the box, then set the selector to Spanish. The easy way is to let your AI do the translating for you. Ask Claude to translate your line, paste the result into Voicebox, switch the selector to match, and generate. Now it is genuinely your voice speaking fluent Spanish, Japanese, or German, not English with a strange accent. One more tip: write with real punctuation. Periods, question marks, and exclamation points all change how alive the delivery sounds. 05 GIVE CLAUDE YOUR VOICE Voicebox has a built in connector so Claude Code can speak through it. With Voicebox open, run this once in Terminal to connect them: claude mcp add voicebox http://127.0.0.1:17493/mcp \ --transport http \ --header "X-Voicebox-Client-Id: claude-code" \ -s user Then open Voicebox Settings, go to the MCP tab, and bind your voice profile to the claude-code client. That tells Claude to always speak in your cloned voice instead of a default one. Voicebox has to stay open for this to work, the connector only lives while the app is running. 06 MAKE CLAUDE TALK BACK The connector only loads when a Claude session starts, so open a fresh Claude Code window. Give it any task, and add one line to your request: When you are done, use the voicebox speak tool to tell me what you did. Claude finishes the job, then your Mac reads the summary out loud in your own voice. That is the whole trick. Your AI stops being a wall of text and starts talking with you. I F A C L O N E E V E R S O U N D S F L A T It is almost always the sample, not a setting. There are no hidden emotion sliders. Re-record the sample with more energy and the output follows. Flat sample in, flat voice out. Lively sample in, lively voice out. A C T I O N A B L E A I · J O I N T H E C O M M U N I T Y You just gave your AI a voice. Come build the rest with us.
